summary: Volume 1 of the English translation of Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's Mahan Kosh, the standard encyclopaedia of Sikh literature, published by the Publication Bureau of Punjabi University, Patiala. An alphabetical reference work of Sikh works and their authors, with biographical notes and dates. The most heavily used title in this library.

Volume 2 of the English translation of Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's Mahan Kosh (Encyclopaedia of the Sikh Literature), published by the Publication Bureau, Punjabi University, Patiala. Continues the alphabetical reference work from Volume 1; it is a separate instalment rather than an excerpt of it.

Volume 3 of the English translation of Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's Mahan Kosh, published by the Publication Bureau, Punjabi University, Patiala. Its title page carries the translator's imprint in both Gurmukhi and Latin script. The third instalment of the alphabetical encyclopaedia of Sikh literature.

Volume 1 of Sri Gur Panth Prakash by Rattan Singh Bhangoo, in English translation by Kulwant Singh, published by the Nanaksahi Institute of Sikh Studies, Chandigarh. Covers episodes 1 to 81. The work tells the history of the Guru's life as a sequence of episodes rather than chapters, and is the fullest account we hold of how the early Sikh community developed.

Volume 2 of Sri Gur Panth Prakash by Rattan Singh Bhangoo, English translation by Kulwant Singh, Nanaksahi Institute of Sikh Studies, Chandigarh. Covers episodes 82 to 169. Together with Volume 1 this reaches episode 169 of the work's 1,123.

Opens with the Kalambod (kabot) by Bhai Nand Lal, the earliest known work on Gurmukhi grammar, written around 1600 as a primer for learning the script. The teacher's comments are printed with it, including the note that these are all words of love and affection, and that wrong meanings should be checked when writing. Despite the catalogue title, this is one of the most important early Punjabi texts in existence.

Santa Singh's printed edition of the Sarbloh Granth (Sarab Loh Granth Sahib), a voluminous scripture of some 6,500 poetic stanzas arranged in five sections (adhiyas). The text opens with the lines 'char bodh khat astadas, karam dharam sach naam' and gives the instruction 'tai upaav'. Traditionally attributed to Guru Gobind Singh and revered above all by the Nihang order, though its authorship is genuinely disputed by scholars.

A school grammar and composition book in Punjabi, this edition compiled by Narinder Singh Duggal after Ved Agni-Hotri Tarkara's standard nineteenth-century grammar. The contents cover spelling (lagakhar), letters (shabod-vod), grammar, exercises, varan-bo and letter-writing (pat badh dha na).

An anthology of vaar, the sung martial and devotional anthems central to Sikh public worship. The contents name two by title, Vaar Sarbloh Ki and Vaar Bhagat Baschal Ki, together with bhamika and bir ras. Publisher listed as Tattakar.

A month-long beginner's course in Punjabi, structured rather than a reference work. The contents run through joining consonants, pronunciation, verbs, adjectives, postpositions, degrees of comparison, and the remaining parts of speech.

Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth by Kavi Santokh Singh, a masnavi-style telling of the life of Guru Gobind Singh. Our copy's opening is the alphabetical index, keyed by the first word of each poem in the Punjabi manner: kabir (bhagat), up pran, umdhatu tvarikh, urvashi, oghavti (sarasvati), ashat khand, ashat guru chamtakar.

Volume 9 of the Universal Encyclopaedia (Punjabi Vishav Kosh), edited at Oxford University Press, Patiala by Jagjit Kaur, Jasbir Kaur and Harjit Kaur. The preface states the work's purpose plainly: to make universal knowledge available through a single reference, superseding the many separate dictionaries. A general-knowledge encyclopaedia rather than a Sikh-only one.

Volume 10 of the Universal Encyclopaedia (Punjabi Vishav Kosh), edited at Oxford University Press, Patiala. This volume covers a letter range running from the Encyclopaedia of Urdu and Americana through religion and verses, insect-pests of crops, and the Imperial Gazetteer of India.

The Janam Sakhi of Bhai Bala, printed at Untalvi, Amritsar, with uchast (opening verses). Bhai Bala's is the earliest of the Janam Sakhis, predating the split into the rival manuscript families that came later, and it carries the earliest account of Guru Nanak's life.

The poems of Mian Muhammad Bakhsh Qadri, the seventeenth-century Punjabi Sufi poet whose kalam shaped the vocabulary of Punjabi devotional writing and who is much quoted within Sikh scripture. Our copy is a 112-page edition digitised by Maktabah.org. The scanned text was too poorly printed for us to read directly, so this description rests on the title page alone.

A life of Guru Gobind Singh, in the sau sakhI ('hundred companions') tradition of hagiography. The scanned text could not be read, so this description rests on the title alone and we cannot yet say more about its contents or author.

A work on Anandpur Sahib. The scan is a poor microfilm copy and its text could not be read at all, so we cannot describe its contents, author or period. Recovering this one needs either a better scan or a different copy of the text.
A Punjabi novel. The scan's text could not be read, so the author, plot and period are unknown to us from the book itself.
A collection of bhagat, the devotional poetry of the Sikh saints. Only fragments of the text could be read, so its extent and contents are not yet established.
Title translates as 'writer' or 'author'. No text could be retrieved for this item, so nothing further can be said about it from the book itself.
